query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the nanoscale dispersion and size of in situ TiB2 particles in the HEA coating governs simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance by promoting grain refinement that impedes dislocation motion and providing abundant, uniformly distributed nucleation sites for a coherent passive film that resists localized breakdown.
generation.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy coating produced by laser cladding with no or excessive boron addition, leading to either coarse or inhomogeneously distributed TiB2.
generation.intervention: Introduce a precisely controlled, trace amount of boron (near x = 0.5) during laser cladding to yield a uniform dispersion of ultrafine TiB2 precipitates.
generation.conditions: Coatings are produced under identical laser cladding parameters, with only the boron content adjusted to target ultrafine particle formation in a harsh corrosive mechanical environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl with imposed sliding wear).
generation.structural_mediator: A significantly refined and homogeneous microstructure with nanoscale TiB2 precipitates and smaller BCC grain sizes.
generation.mechanism: The ultrafine TiB2 particles act as barriers to dislocation motion (enhancing wear resistance by impeding plastic deformation) and serve as effective nucleation sites for stable, adherent passive films (reducing localized corrosion initiation). The refined grains further contribute by creating more grain boundaries that can slow corrosion pathways and impede crack propagation under cyclic mechanical loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline with either no B or excessive B (leading to coarse TiB2), the optimized coating will exhibit a significantly lower wear rate (potentially reduced by similar orders as S2–S3 in the paper) and a lower corrosion current density (with icorr reduced by around 50% relative to non-optimized coatings).
generation.baseline: Coatings produced with either no boron (coarser microstructure) or with excessive boron resulting in agglomerated TiB2 which promotes stress concentration and defective passive films.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold when the processing parameters ensure full melting/solidification control and homogeneity; however, if the laser cladding process introduces other uncontrolled defects or if the aggressive environment exceeds the stability limits of the passive film, the benefit may be diminished.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in wear rate and corrosion current is uncertain, though the trend is expected to follow the comparative improvements seen in the optimized S2–S3 compositions reported in the paper.

paper_did: Synthesized as‐cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 high‐entropy alloy by arc melting and prepared samples according to ASTM G32-10 standards.
Conducted cavitation erosion (CE) experiments in both 3.5 wt% NaCl solution and deionized water, measuring cumulative mass loss, mass loss rates, and surface roughness.

Characterized the microstructure via XRD, EBSD, and SEM-EDS to reveal a dual-phase system with a dominant FCC phase and intermetallic σ and μ phases, and measured local hardness using Vickers microhardness testing.

Performed electrochemical tests (potentiodynamic polarization, open-circuit potential, and electrochemical noise with wavelet analysis) to elucidate corrosion behavior and passive film dynamics under CE conditions.
paper_reported: That the overall CE damage in the corrosive 3.5 wt% NaCl medium is significantly greater than in deionized water, with selective phase degradation where the softer FCC phase is preferentially removed.

An increasing trend in hardness over prolonged CE time due to work hardening, and a demonstrable synergy between cavitation-induced mechanical damage and corrosion (with the synergy contributing ~48.02% of the total mass loss).
That the evolution of the passive film is dynamic, as evidenced by periodic OCP shifts and EN analysis, with localized breakdown at the interfaces between the FCC matrix and intermetallic phases.
paper_proposed: While not explicitly listing future experiments, the study’s discussion implies that further improvement in CE-corrosion resistance might be achieved by tailoring microstructural features – such as reducing selective phase corrosion – and by designing new alloys with enhanced passive film formation.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in HEAs is governed by an adaptive work‐hardening mechanism where the preferential removal of the softer FCC phase under mechanical impact induces a dense, strain‐hardened surface layer that improves passive film formation and reduces localized corrosion.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase microstructure, featuring a softer FCC matrix interspersed with harder intermetallic σ and μ phases.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a pre-conditioning mechanical treatment (e.g., controlled shot peening) to pre-induce nanocrystallization and work hardening in the FCC matrix at the surface prior to exposure to combined wear and corrosive environments.
hypotheses.conditions: Testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under cyclic cavitation erosion (CE) conditions comparable to those described in the paper.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A refined, strain-hardened surface microstructure with improved passive film repair dynamics.
hypotheses.mechanism: The intervention accelerates the formation of a dense work-hardened layer by intensifying dislocation density in the FCC phase. This layer better withstands mechanical removal, supports a robust passive oxide film, and minimizes the formation of microcracks at phase boundaries that normally serve as corrosion initiation sites. Consequently, a synergy between wear-induced work hardening and corrosion resistance emerges.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The pre-treated sample will exhibit a reduced cumulative mass loss (both from mechanical wear and corrosion-induced degradation) when compared to the untreated baseline by approximately a moderate margin (direction supported qualitatively by increased hardness data and passive film stability, although precise values are uncertain).
hypotheses.baseline: As-cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA without pre-treatment exhibiting conventional CE-induced selective phase corrosion as described in PMC11378927::web::012::morphologies_and_roughness_of_cocrfenimo.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism should hold when the wear intensity is sufficient to activate work hardening in the FCC phase but not so high as to remove the entire surface layer; it might fail under extreme CE conditions that prevent any passive film recovery.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in mass loss and distribution of strain-hardened phases is not precisely known.

hypotheses.what_is_new: Introducing a pre-treatment mechanical work-hardening step to deliberately induce an adaptive protective layer that mitigates the synergistic interplay between wear and corrosion, a strategy not explored in the referenced study.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is controlled by the extent of intermetallic phase formation; specifically, reducing the volume fraction of the selectively corroding intermetallic (σ and μ) phases by compositional modification enhances uniform passive film behavior and lowers galvanic coupling effects that drive localized corrosion during wear.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA exhibiting significant precipitation of σ and μ intermetallic phases embedded within an FCC matrix.
hypotheses.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by reducing Mo content (or adjusting the Mo-to-Cr ratio) to decrease the precipitation of σ and μ phases, thereby enhancing the uniformity of the FCC matrix.
hypotheses.conditions: Testing under identical cavitation erosion-corrosion conditions in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, keeping other processing parameters constant.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A more homogeneous FCC microstructure with fewer intermetallic particles that act as local galvanic cells.
hypotheses.mechanism: The modified composition suppresses intermetallic precipitation, reducing micro-galvanic corrosion and the preferential chemical attack at phase boundaries. A more uniform FCC phase facilitates stable passive layer formation under wear conditions, thereby diminishing the synergistic degradation observed previously.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The compositionally modified alloy is expected to show a lower overall mass loss under combined wear and corrosion conditions relative to the baseline alloy, with less pitting and reduced OCP variability. The improvement is predicted qualitatively, though the exact magnitude is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: As-cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA with higher Mo, which exhibits notable intermetallic precipitation and associated localized corrosion as detailed in PMC11378927::web::010::microstructure_characterization_of_cocrf.
hypotheses.boundary: The prediction holds as long as the reduced Mo does not compromise overall strength or other desirable properties; if mechanical properties degrade excessively, the improved corrosion behavior may not translate to higher overall resistance.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the trade-off between reduced intermetallic fraction and potential loss of hardness or strength.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the stability and uniformity of the passive film, which critically depends on microstructural homogeneity; homogenizing the microstructure via post-casting solution treatment can eliminate compositional gradients and intermetallic precipitates that serve as weak links for passive film breakdown.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-cast HEA with heterogeneous microstructure featuring compositional segregation and pronounced intermetallic phases (σ and μ) interspersed within the FCC matrix.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a post-casting solution treatment (homogenization annealing) process to dissolve or reduce the intermetallic phases and achieve a more uniform single-phase FCC microstructure.
hypotheses.conditions: Carry out cavitation erosion-corrosion tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under conditions similar to those in the original study.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A homogenized microstructure with minimized chemical inhomogeneities that supports a more continuous and defect-free passive film.
hypotheses.mechanism: The solution treatment minimizes local compositional differences and removes or reduces the size and quantity of intermetallic precipitates. This uniform microstructure reduces the formation of micro-galvanic cells and sites of preferential passive film breakdown under mechanical stress, thereby enhancing the overall resistance to concurrent wear and corrosion.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The homogenized HEA should display improved resistance against both mechanical erosion and corrosion, reflected by lower cumulative mass loss, more stable OCP behavior, and less severe surface pitting compared to the as-cast condition. hypotheses.boundary: The effectiveness of the solution treatment is contingent upon sufficient homogenization without over-softening the material; under conditions where complete dissolution of intermetallics is not achieved, the benefits may be reduced.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Exact improvement metrics (e.g., mass loss reduction percentage) are uncertain and need experimental determination.

paper_did: Synthesized a CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy via powder metallurgy techniques including mechanical alloying (30 h milling), cold pressing, sintering at 1100 °C, and subsequent machining into electrodes.
Deposited successive layers of the alloy onto 316L stainless steel substrates using electro spark deposition under argon atmosphere, targeting a coating thickness of 25–100 µm.

Characterized the coatings with SEM, EDS, and XRD to observe the microstructure (including a homogeneous region near the substrate, upper-layer porosity, and the formation of σ and μ intermetallic phases), and performed pull‐off adhesion tests.

Evaluated corrosion behavior with potentiodynamic polarization in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature, reporting a very low corrosion rate (0.00016 mm/year) along with evidence of passivation (partial filling of surface pores).
paper_reported: The deposited CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating exhibited excellent adhesion on stainless steel with a measured pull‐off strength of ~0.67 MPa and a continuous, bonded layer near the substrate.

XRD analysis indicated that the coating underwent phase transformations during the electro spark deposition process, showing an increased content of σ (rich in Co, Cr, Fe) and μ (rich in Mo) phases relative to the sintered bulk.

Corrosion tests in saline solution demonstrated markedly low corrosion rates, with the formation of a passivating layer (likely associated with chromium segregation) that progressively filled the surface pores.
paper_proposed: The paper suggests that high-entropy alloy coatings like CoCrFeNiMo0.85 are promising candidates for corrosion protection in aggressive environments (e.g., geothermal applications).

It hints at future investigations to further optimize processing parameters and microstructural features (such as controlling porosity and phase distribution) to enhance the durability and corrosion resistance of the coatings.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The simultaneous wear–corrosion resistance of high-entropy alloys is governed by the rapid formation and self-healing of a Mo/Cr-enriched passivating film on newly exposed surfaces during wear events.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A mechanically alloyed CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy with inherent microsegregation of Mo and Cr and a coating produced via electro spark deposition that exhibits some porosity.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a controlled mild mechanical pre-conditioning (or lower intensity abrasive pre-treatment) to intentionally expose fresh surfaces, promoting in situ segregation of Mo and Cr. Alternatively, locally modify surface chemistry via a light pre-oxidation step to favor passivation.
hypotheses.conditions: Testing in a saline environment (3.5 wt.% NaCl) under cyclic abrasion that simulates simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosion. The controlled comparison would be between a sample with the tailored surface exposure that enhances passivation versus a baseline unmodified alloy coating.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, uniform Mo/Cr-rich oxide layer that rapidly reforms over wear-induced surfaces, filling micro-pores and preventing corrosive ingress.
hypotheses.mechanism: Wear events expose fresh alloy surfaces where Mo and Cr quickly diffuse to form a passivating oxide film. This film acts as a barrier to both continued corrosive attack and abrasive wear by reducing localized degradation. The self-healing nature of the film maintains protection under cyclic wear conditions.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The pre-conditioned sample should exhibit lower cumulative mass loss and reduced corrosion current density under simultaneous wear–corrosion testing, with an estimated improvement in performance (directionally lower degradation rates) when compared to an unmodified baseline. The effect is expected to be significant if the passivation kinetics are sufficiently fast.
hypotheses.baseline: The standard CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating deposited by electro spark deposition without a pre-conditioning treatment.
hypotheses.boundary: This hypothesis should hold in environments where wear is moderate enough to allow re-passivation of fresh surfaces. Under extremely aggressive mechanical loads that remove the passivating film faster than it can reform, the benefit would diminish.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvement is supported, the precise quantitative reduction in degradation rates is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-conditioned sample does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both wear and corrosion degradation compared to the baseline, or shows faster degradation due to unstable passivation, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the observed formation of passivating layers (passivation filling pores) in CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coatings (PMC8305802::web::014) combined with principles of self-healing passive films in corrosion-resistant materials.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It explicitly links the rapid re-passivation due to Mo and Cr segregation, triggered by wear exposure, to enhanced simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance—a mechanism not directly tested in the paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The dual-phase microstructure, featuring dispersed hard σ and μ intermetallic phases embedded in a softer FCC matrix, improves resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion by impeding both mechanical abrasion and the ingress paths for corrosive agents.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy with a mixed FCC/BCC matrix and precipitated intermetallic phases as produced by mechanical alloying and electro spark deposition.
hypotheses.intervention: Employ a modified heat treatment (post-deposition annealing at controlled temperatures) to fine-tune and increase the volume fraction and distribution uniformity of the hard σ and μ phases within the FCC matrix.
hypotheses.conditions: Expose both the heat-treated and standard samples to simultaneous wear–corrosion conditions; for instance, a 3.5 wt.% NaCl saline environment combined with a controlled abrasive particle slurry environment.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: An optimized distribution of hard intermetallic phases acting as micro-reinforcements that locally block crack propagation and reduce channel formation for corrosive solution infiltration.
hypotheses.mechanism: The hard phases serve as mechanical barriers that improve wear resistance by bearing high loads and reducing plastic deformation, while their chemical stability minimizes galvanic differential with the matrix. This dual role restricts pathways for corrosive agents, thereby reducing corrosion under wear conditions.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The heat-treated (optimized phase fraction) sample is predicted to show lower wear track penetration depths and lower corrosion current densities relative to the untreated baseline. Improvement should manifest as slower progressive material loss when both abrasive forces and corrosive solutions are present.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-deposited CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating with its natural mix of phases.

paper_did: Fabricated an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with a coarse-grained (~42 µm) microstructure by laser-based additive manufacturing using gas‐atomized powder.

Conducted sliding contact experiments in an ultra‐high vacuum (UHV ~10⁻⁹ torr) environment with a sapphire (Al₂O₃) sphere at two different normal loads (10 mN and 100 mN) to study stress‐dependent friction behavior.
Measured steady‐state friction coefficients (approximately 0.32 at low load and 0.68 at high load) and determined wear rates (as low as ~10⁻⁶ mm³/N-m) via high-resolution interferometry.

Performed detailed microstructural characterization using STEM/TEM to demonstrate the formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline (and partially amorphous) near-surface layer with grain sizes as small as 2–3 nm, underpinning evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior.

Utilized a dynamic amorphization model to predict the grain size-dependent shear strength (relating friction to surface shear strength) and estimated the average high angle grain boundary energy (~0.87 J/m²) for the alloy.
paper_reported: That under high strain rate sliding in an inert (UHV) environment, severe plastic deformation leads to dynamic amorphization and extreme grain refinement (into the inverse Hall-Petch regime), which in turn lowers the friction coefficient and results in exceptionally low wear rates.
A clear correlation between friction coefficient, shear strength (derived from the bulk hardness), and the refined near-surface grain size was established and validated by TEM measurements.

The paper also quantified grain growth effects (e.g., friction coefficient increases upon a pause in sliding) and used the dynamic amorphization model as a predictive tool for shear strength and grain size effects.
paper_proposed: While no explicit future experiments are detailed, the discussion implies that further exploration of the dynamic amorphization model could extend to optimizing friction and wear behavior via controlled surface grain refinement, and that understanding grain boundary energy and cavitation (nanoporosity) may offer insights into superplasticity and failure mechanisms.

hypotheses.mechanism: The severe plastic deformation under sliding refines the grain size into the inverse Hall-Petch regime, reducing the shear strength locally and lowering friction and wear. This dual-effect limits both mechanical degradation and electrochemical attack.

paper_did: Fabricated AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx high‐entropy alloy coatings (with x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding, using high‐purity gas-atomized elemental powders.
Introduced boron as a microalloying element to react in situ with Ti to form TiB2 particles, thereby modifying the microstructure without changing the base BCC and σ phases.

Conducted extensive microstructural characterization (XRD, SEM, EDS), microhardness measurements, tribological wear tests (using a 20 N load for 30 min with a YG6 ball), and electrochemical corrosion tests (potentiodynamic polarization and EIS in 3.5 wt.% NaCl) under room temperature conditions.
paper_reported: Found that boron addition leads to the in situ formation of TiB2, with increased B content refining the BCC phase and increasing both the fraction and size of TiB2.

Reported that coatings with moderate B addition (S2 at x = 0.5 for corrosion and S3 at x = 1 for wear) exhibited enhanced microhardness, reduced wear rate, and improved corrosion resistance, while excessive boron (x = 1.5) caused TiB2 agglomeration, spalling, and degraded performance.

Elucidated mechanisms where fine TiB2 particles reinforce the matrix (impeding dislocation motion) and contribute to passive film stability, whereas coarsened particles lead to defects that accelerate film breakdown.
paper_proposed: Suggested that further optimization could be achieved through compositional tuning and post-processing strategies to address specific service environments, machinability, and long-term stability.

paper_did: Developed and deposited two high‐entropy alloy coatings (CoCrFeNiMo0.85 [Mo-HEA] and Al0.5CoCrFeNi [Al-HEA]) via laser metal deposition (LMD) on different substrates (carbon steel S235JR, stainless steels 316L and 304L).
Tested the coatings in three different geothermal exposure conditions – a wellhead test, an aerated test, and an erosion test – at the Hellisheidi geothermal power plant.

Characterized the coatings before and after exposure using microstructural and chemical tools (SEM, BSE, EDS, optical microscopy, and optical profilometry) to evaluate manufacturing defects (e.g., cracks, porosity), corrosion products, oxide film formation, and erosion damage.
paper_reported: Observed that manufacturing defects, especially cracks in the coatings (notably in Mo-HEA on carbon steel and in Al-HEA on 304L), promote localized erosion-corrosion damage.

Found that Mo-HEA coatings on stainless steel (316L) exhibited fewer defects and superior corrosion resistance, with formation of a partial Cr-O-rich passive film, whereas Al-HEA coatings showed more extensive general and localized corrosion along with deep erosion pits.
Noted galvanic effects at the interface when a Mo-HEA coating on carbon steel produced iron-based corrosion products likely linked to dissimilar substrate chemistry and thermal expansion mismatches.
paper_proposed: Optimizing the formulation and production process of the CoCrFeNiMo0.85 (Mo-HEA) coating to eliminate or substantially reduce manufacturing-induced cracking, particularly when deposited on carbon steel substrates.
A general recommendation to improve coating integrity and thereby enhance the resistance against simultaneous erosion and corrosion in harsh geothermal environments.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Eliminating processing‐induced defects (especially cracks) enables the formation of a continuous, mechanically robust passive oxide film on HEA surfaces which governs simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: LMD-deposited CoCrFeNiMo0.85 HEA coatings that as-deposited on carbon steel or stainless steel substrates may contain manufacturing cracks/porosity.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a post-deposition annealing or hot isostatic pressing (HIP) step to heal cracks and reduce residual stresses in the HEA coating.
hypotheses.conditions: Test in simulated geothermal fluid environments (deaerated and aerated conditions) with superimposed mechanical erosive impacts; perform comparisons between as-deposited and annealed/HIP-treated samples.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The integrity of the passive Cr-O-rich oxide film formed on the HEA surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: By reducing manufacturing defects, stress concentrations that lead to film rupture or discontinuous oxide layers are minimized. A continuous passive oxide film (observed in aerated tests in Mo-HEA coatings on stainless steel, e.g., PMC8200011::web::009 and PMC8200011::web::019) acts as both a corrosion barrier and a mechanical buffer, reducing the initiation sites for erosive wear. The improved adhesion and continuity mitigate the synergistic effects where microcracks accelerate material removal.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The annealed/HIP-treated HEA samples will exhibit a lower combined degradation rate (both wear and corrosion) compared to as-deposited samples, with a measurable improvement (uncertain magnitude) in passive film continuity and coating thickness retention.
hypotheses.baseline: As-deposited LMD HEA coatings that show manufacturing cracks and discontinuous passive films (e.g., Mo-HEA on carbon steel, as reported in PMC8200011::web::003 and PMC8200011::web::015).
hypotheses.boundary: The protective effect should be significant under moderate erosive conditions and in fluids where passive film formation is operative; however, at extreme mechanical impacts or highly aggressive chemical conditions, the benefit may diminish.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement is uncertain, as the exact relationship between defect healing and passive film stability under cyclic erosion-corrosion remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA-coated samples on the same substrate: one set as-deposited and one subjected to post-deposition annealing/HIP. Expose both sets to identical simulated geothermal conditions with a standardized mechanical erosion apparatus.
measurements: Surface morphology and continuity of the oxide film (via SEM/BSE/EDS)
Coating thickness before and after exposure (optical profilometry)
Weight loss or pit depth analysis as a measure of combined degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed/HIP-treated samples do not show statistically significant reduction in wear-corrosion degradation (no improvement in oxide continuity or damage metrics) compared to the as-deposited samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observation that manufacturing cracks (PMC8200011::web::003, PMC8200011::web::015) promote local erosion-corrosion damage via enhanced fluid turbulence and galvanic effects.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes an active post-processing treatment to heal inherent deposition defects to yield a mechanically robust oxide film under simultaneous erosive and corrosive stresses—a concept not examined in the paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Enhanced wear-corrosion resistance in HEAs is governed by the ability to promote beneficial elemental segregation (specifically Mo enrichment) at the near-surface regions that stabilizes a high-adherence, protective oxide scale.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: LMD-deposited high-entropy alloy coatings such as CoCrFeNiMo0.85 with a nominal homogeneous distribution of alloying elements.
hypotheses.intervention: Modify the laser deposition parameters or introduce a subsequent surface alloying step to induce preferential Mo segregation at the top 10–20 µm of the coating.
hypotheses.conditions: Expose modified and unmodified HEA samples to corrosive environments with mechanical wear (simulated geothermal fluid with erosive impact) under closely controlled temperature and pressure conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The composition and adherence of the Mo-rich intermetallic or oxide scale (e.g., a Mo-enriched oxide layer) at the surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: Molybdenum is known to improve corrosion resistance in HEAs by contributing to passivity. By promoting Mo segregation near the surface, a more stable and adherent Mo-rich oxide scale forms. This scale is less susceptible to wear-induced removal and provides a dual function: resisting both chemical attack and mechanical abrasion. The mechanism is analogous to the enhanced performance seen in Mo-HEA coatings without manufacturing cracks (PMC8200011::web::009, PMC8200011::web::020).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: HEA samples with engineered Mo-surface enrichment will demonstrate lower rates of combined corrosion and wear degradation compared to unmodified HEAs, with improvements manifested as a reduced number and depth of erosion pits and a more continuous oxide layer.
hypotheses.baseline: Standard LMD-deposited HEA coatings with nominal elemental distribution, as seen in the base level experiments in the paper.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism should be effective in environments where the oxide formation kinetics allow the Mo-rich scale to form and remain adherent; if the environment’s chemistry favors dissolution of Mo oxides, the benefit may be reduced.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimal degree of Mo segregation and its exact impact on scaling kinetics under simultaneous mechanical loading is not fully established.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s evidence that Mo-HEA coatings show good resistance when free from defects (PMC8200011::web::009, PMC8200011::web::015) and the known role of Mo in enhancing passivity in corrosion literature.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the paper's concept by suggesting a deliberate compositional modification—targeted Mo enrichment—to actively enhance the adhesion and robustness of the protective oxide scale under simultaneous degradation.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The resistance of HEAs to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the quality of the interface between the HEA coating and its substrate, where a graded interlayer reduces galvanic potential differences and improves stress transfer, thereby minimizing localized degradation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: HEA coatings deposited via LMD on substrates with significant differences in thermal expansion and composition (e.g., carbon steel vs. stainless steel), which can lead to interfacial microcracks and galvanic effects.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a compositionally graded interlayer between the substrate and the HEA coating (or adjust deposition parameters to achieve a graded interface) to better match the thermal expansion coefficients and reduce electrochemical potential differences.
hypotheses.conditions: Conduct comparative tests on samples with and without graded interfaces under simulated geothermal environments that impose both corrosive chemical attack and mechanical erosive loads.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The integrity and electrochemical compatibility at the HEA/substrate interface, as evidenced by reduced microcracking and minimized galvanic coupling.
hypotheses.mechanism: A graded interlayer minimizes sharp compositional and thermal expansion mismatches that lead to microcracking and localized galvanic corrosion (as observed in the carbon steel–HEA interface in PMC8200011::web::017). Improved interface integrity will reduce the initiation sites for combined damage from wear and corrosion. By reducing interfacial defects, the passive film continuity over the entire coating-substrate system is maintained under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: HEA coatings with a graded interface will show lower interfacial crack densities, reduced galvanic corrosion indicators (e.g., less iron-based corrosion product formation), and lower overall combined degradation compared to coatings deposited directly on a dissimilar substrate.
hypotheses.baseline: Traditional LMD-deposited HEA coatings on substrates with abrupt compositional and thermal mismatches (e.g., Mo-HEA on carbon steel, which exhibited galvanic effects in PMC8200011::web::017).
hypotheses.boundary: The effectiveness of the graded interface is expected to be most pronounced when the substrate mismatch is substantial. In cases where the substrate is already compatible (e.g., stainless steel), the graded layer may offer marginal benefits.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the role of substrate compatibility is well understood, the quantitative impact of a graded interlayer on simultaneous wear and corrosion under dynamic geothermal conditions remains to be fully established.

Detection of galvanic corrosion indicators (via EDS mapping of corrosion products)

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graded-interface samples do not demonstrate reduced interfacial degradation (microcracking, galvanic corrosion markers) and improved overall wear-corrosion resistance compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The observation in the paper that substrate–HEA interfaces can significantly influence degradation (PMC8200011::web::017) and fundamentals of galvanic corrosion (TXT::wikipedia::Galvanic_corrosion::015).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely proposes that engineering a graded interface can mitigate the synergistic effects of wear and corrosion by reducing interfacial stress and galvanic coupling—a factor not addressed by the original paper.

testable.reason: A controlled experiment comparing as-deposited coatings with samples subjected to post-deposition annealing or HIP (with standardized erosive–corrosive testing and subsequent microstructural/oxidation assessments) readily allows quantification of performance differences.

paper_did: Fabricated an amorphous AlTiVNb high‐entropy alloy (HEA) film on Si substrates using magnetron sputtering under specific conditions (100 W, 0.5 Pa, Argon at 30 sccm, 90 mm target-to-substrate distance), yielding a 1.4 μm thick film.
Characterized the film’s microstructure via SEM, AFM, XRD, and TEM, and observed a distinct island structure on the surface along with an amorphous phase.

Measured mechanical properties through nanoindentation (yielding a hardness of ~5.7 GPa and modulus of ~110.7 GPa) and compression tests on FIB-fabricated pillars (showing a high compressive strength of 3.6 GPa and plasticity of 58%), attributing high strength to chemical disorder, nanostructure, and lattice distortion and high ductility to ductile shear bands and the island morphology.
Evaluated corrosion resistance using Tafel polarization in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, finding a current density of 4.90 × 10⁻⁸ A/cm² and potential of −0.234 V comparable to 316L stainless steel.
paper_reported: A lightweight, amorphous AlTiVNb HEA film exhibiting a low density (5.67 g/cm³) with excellent mechanical performance (high strength of 3.6 GPa, high plasticity of 58%, hardness ~5.7 GPa, modulus ~110.7 GPa) and corrosion resistance in NaCl solution.

The high strength was explained by a combination of the disordered state, nanostructure, and lattice distortion effects, while high ductility was linked to the formation of ductile shear bands and the unique island structure.

Corrosion resistance was attributed to the chemical disorder state, cocktail effect, and homogeneous amorphous structure, with additional notes on how the island morphology might influence surface area and oxidation behavior.
paper_proposed: The paper suggests future applications of the high-performance HEA film in flexible microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials without testing the synergistic effects of combined wear and corrosion or exploring modification of the film’s nanostructure through processing parameter variations.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The synergistic resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the island‐structured amorphous morphology that enables continuous re‐passivation. Under combined mechanical and corrosive attack, the nanostructured islands continuously shed and regenerate a protective oxide layer, which limits the progression of both wear damage and corrosion attack.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Amorphous AlTiVNb HEA film with an island structure as deposited by magnetron sputtering.
hypotheses.intervention: Modify the sputtering processing conditions (for example, adjust working pressure or target-to-substrate distance) to vary the prominence and spacing of the island structures while keeping overall composition constant.
hypotheses.conditions: Prepare two sets of films: one with the island morphology optimized (as in the baseline paper) and another with a suppressed island structure (more uniform surface) achieved via adjusted deposition conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Nanostructured island morphology that facilitates localized oxidation and rapid passivation.
hypotheses.mechanism: The island structure creates a larger effective surface area with repeated topological features that, upon mechanical wear, expose fresh surfaces that rapidly form a passivating oxide layer due to the alloy’s chemical disorder and cocktail effect. This self-renewing passivation reduces the active sites for corrosion while simultaneously distributing wear-induced stress.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Under simultaneous wear-corrosion testing, the optimized island-structure sample will show lower material loss and reduced depth of wear-corrosion damage than the uniform sample. The wear component may be reduced by about 10–20% and the corrosion current density lowered correspondingly, though precise magnitude is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-deposited amorphous HEA film with its intrinsic island structure as described in PMC9735962.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold when the island features are on the order of a few hundred nanometers; if deposition conditions lead to either overly coarse islands or a completely uniform film, the rapid re-passivation may not occur, and the hypothesis may fail.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement in wear-corrosion resistance is not precisely predictable without further experimental calibration.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding that the amorphous AlTiVNb HEA film exhibits excellent corrosion resistance and high mechanical performance due to its nanostructure and island morphology (PMC9735962).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis specifically links the island morphology to simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance by proposing that the morphology drives continuous oxide re-passivation, a mechanism not directly explored in the paper.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Nanovoids within the amorphous matrix act as stress absorbers and barriers to electrolyte ingress, thereby governing resistance to combined wear and corrosion. A high density of well-distributed nano-voids mitigates stress concentration during wear and limits pathways for corrosive species, reducing the overall degradation rate.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Amorphous high-entropy alloy film (AlTiVNb) exhibiting inherent small, high-density voids and island structures as observed in the baseline study.
hypotheses.intervention: Alter the magnetron sputtering deposition parameters (e.g., varying the working pressure or deposition rate) to systematically vary the density and distribution of nanovoids while maintaining the composition and overall amorphous structure.
hypotheses.conditions: Manufacture two series of films: one with a higher density of nanovoids (achieved at, for instance, a higher working pressure) and a counterpart with minimized void density (lower working pressure or optimized adatom mobility). Both series should be subjected to identical wear-corrosion tests.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The nanovoids and associated island structures that modulate stress distribution and serve as barriers to corrosive liquid penetration.
hypotheses.mechanism: Under mechanical loading, clusters of nanovoids absorb and redistribute applied stresses, reducing local hot spots that can trigger crack initiation. Concurrently, the nanovoids interrupt continuous pathways for the ingress of corrosive electrolytes, delaying the onset of corrosion, particularly along wear-induced cracks. This dual role reduces overall material loss when wear and corrosion occur simultaneously.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Films with an optimized, higher nanovoid density are expected to display lower combined degradation (both reduced wear volume and lower corrosion rates) compared to films with few or no nanovoids. Predicted improvements may be on the order of a modest reduction (tentatively 10–20% lower degradation) though the magnitude is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: The standard magnetron-sputtered amorphous AlTiVNb HEA film, as characterized in PMC9735962.
hypotheses.boundary: The hypothesis holds when nanovoids are present in controlled densities; if the void density is too high, it may compromise mechanical integrity, or if too low, the stress absorption and barrier effects may be negligible.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the qualitative effect is supported by the role of nanovoids in stress distribution, the precise optimal void density and the quantitative improvement remain uncertain.

The formation of ductile shear bands enables effective strain distribution under mechanical load, thereby reducing localized damage and limiting the exposure of fresh, unpassivated surfaces to corrosive media.

paper_did: Fabricated a lightweight amorphous AlTiVNb high-entropy alloy film via magnetron sputtering on (100) Si wafer substrates using a cast target of equiatomic AlTiVNb.

Employed a suite of characterization techniques—including SEM, AFM, XRD, and TEM/SAED—to confirm an amorphous, island‐structured microstructure; conducted nanoindentation and compressive tests on nanopillars (demonstrating 5.7 GPa hardness, 110.7 GPa modulus, 3.6 GPa strength, and 58% plastic strain); and performed Tafel corrosion tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.
paper_reported: The film exhibits a unique strength–ductility synergy (with compressive strength of 3.6 GPa and nearly 58% plastic strain), where high strength is ascribed to the disordered state, nanostructure, and lattice distortion effect, and high ductility results from ductile shear bands and the island structure.

It shows excellent corrosion resistance (current density of 4.90 × 10⁻⁸ A/cm² and potential of −0.234 V in NaCl solution) comparable to 316L stainless steel, attributed to the chemical disorder, cocktail effect, and homogeneous amorphous structure.
paper_proposed: The study suggests that these high-performance HEA films have potential for flexible microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials, implying future exploration of multifunctional coatings that balance mechanical and anticorrosion performance.

paper_reported: Si addition induces a phase transformation from a predominantly FCC structure to a dual-phase {FCC+BCC} microstructure with an increasing BCC fraction, which refines the dendritic grain structure and leads to enhanced microhardness (e.g., the FeCoNiCuAlSi₂.₀ coating reached 581.05 HV₀.₂).

Enhanced wear resistance is observed with increasing Si content, demonstrated by lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates, with the wear mechanism shifting from adhesive/plastic deformation toward abrasive modes.

Electrochemical tests in NS4 solution show improved corrosion resistance with higher Si content, evidenced by increases in corrosion potential and significant reductions in corrosion current density, attributed to the formation of a protective Al₂O₃ passivation layer.

paper_did: Prepared high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) of compositions AlCoCrFeNi (baseline) and AlCoCrFeNiMo0.25 using high‐purity elemental powders, ball milling, cold pressing, and arc melting with multiple re-melts to ensure homogeneity.

Performed detailed microstructural analyses via X‐ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy‐dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to identify phases (BCC/B2, sigma, and minor FCC) and observe a mosaic-type grain structure (especially upon Mo addition).

Conducted mechanical property assessments using Vickers hardness testing and nanoindentation (measuring hardness, elastic modulus, H/E, H3/E2, elastic recovery index (ERI), and plasticity index (PI)).

Evaluated corrosion resistance by electrochemical techniques (potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) in a 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (~25 °C), estimating parameters such as corrosion current density (icorr) and pitting potential (Epit).
Compared the HEAs with a conventional material (AISI 304L stainless steel) to benchmark improvements in mechanical and corrosion behaviors.
paper_reported: Addition of 5% at. Mo to the AlCoCrFeNi HEA leads to significant microstructural changes: beyond the typical BCC/B2 phase, a small fraction of FCC (≈1%) and the formation of a sigma-phase are observed, along with a refined, mosaic microstructure with smaller, fragmented grains.

Mo addition increases hardness (Vickers and nanoindentation results), the elastic modulus, and improves nanoindentation indices (H/E and H3/E2) as well as the elastic recovery index while reducing the plasticity index, indicating enhanced resistance to wear and plastic deformation.

Electrochemical tests reveal that the Mo-containing HEA exhibits improved corrosion resistance in a 3.5% NaCl environment, which is attributed to microstructural refinements and phase modifications induced by molybdenum.

paper_did: Prepared two high‐entropy alloy variants – one based on AlCoCrFeNi and one with 5% at. Mo addition (AlCoCrFeNiMo0.25) – by arc melting (with remelting for chemical homogeneity) and processed them into disk‐shaped specimens.

Characterized the phase structure and microstructure using X‐ray diffraction (with Williamson–Hall analysis) and scanning electron microscopy with EDS mapping (revealing features such as grain fragmentation, mosaic patterns, and elemental segregation, notably Cr enrichment at grain boundaries).

Measured mechanical properties via Vickers microhardness testing and nanoindentation (obtaining hardness, elastic modulus, and indices such as H/E, H³/E², elastic recovery index, and plasticity index).

Assessed corrosion behavior by performing potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy tests in a 3.5% NaCl solution under ambient conditions, and compared the HEAs with AISI 304L stainless steel as a reference.
paper_reported: The addition of Mo to the AlCoCrFeNi alloy led to significant microstructural changes – the appearance of additional phases (a minor FCC phase and a tetragonal σ‐phase) alongside the disordered BCC phase – and resulted in grain refinement with a fine mosaic pattern.

These microstructural modifications improved the mechanical performance by increasing hardness, elastic modulus, and favorable nanoindentation coefficients (H/E, H³/E², elastic recovery index) while reducing the plasticity index; the enhanced hardness is attributed to both solution hardening and the formation of a σ‐phase.

Corrosion resistance was also improved by the Mo addition, with electrochemical tests (potentiodynamic polarization, EIS) showing lower corrosion current density and higher pitting potential in 3.5% NaCl, which the authors related to a more stable passive film formation influenced by the altered microstructure and chemical segregation.
paper_proposed: While the paper did not explicitly outline a ‘future work’ section, it implicitly suggests that the enhanced properties of the Mo0.25 variant (in terms of both wear resistance and corrosion protection) merit further exploration for use in aggressive, flow‐environment applications – potentially opening avenues for advanced processing or application‐oriented studies.

paper_did: Synthesized an equiatomic CrMoNbTiZr high‐entropy alloy by mixing high‐purity elemental powders under argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C under 40 MPa pressure in vacuum.

Characterized the microstructure using X‐ray diffraction and SEM/EDX, identifying a dual‐phase microstructure consisting mainly of a BCC matrix and a Laves phase, along with in situ formed carbides (NbC and mixed Ti–Mo carbides) resulting from reactions with the graphite die.

Evaluated mechanical properties including Vickers microhardness (global value ~531.5 HV, with phase-specific values of ~365 HV for the BCC phase and ~642 HV for the Laves phase), compressive yield and ultimate strengths (~1110.8 MPa and ~1235.7 MPa, respectively), and an elastic modulus (~34.9 GPa) comparable to cortical bone.
Conducted wear tests using a sliding alumina counterbody (5 N load, 0.1 m/s, 200 m distance) to measure friction (average COF ~0.43) and wear scar (depth ~47 µm, low wear rate).
Performed electrochemical corrosion analyses in PBS and Hanks’ solutions via potentiodynamic polarization, demonstrating effective passivation behavior and low corrosion rates.
paper_reported: The alloy achieved ~97% of its theoretical density with a dual-phase microstructure (BCC matrix and Laves phase) with reinforcing carbides that are associated with enhanced hardness and wear resistance.

Mechanical tests confirmed a high hardness (with distinct phase contributions), high compressive strengths, and a low elastic modulus well‐matched to cortical bone, making the material promising for orthopedic applications.

Wear experiments revealed a moderate coefficient of friction and low wear rate, and corrosion tests in simulated physiological environments indicated rapid passivation and low corrosion current densities.

The discussion attributed the high performance to the tailored microstructure, particularly the beneficial roles of in situ formed carbides and the combination of ductile and hard phases in enhancing both mechanical and electrochemical stability.
paper_proposed: While no separate future work section is presented, the paper hints at improvements in microstructural homogeneity through potential heat treatments to reduce element segregation, and suggests that additional processing steps (such as hot isostatic pressing) could further densify the material and minimize pore‐induced localized corrosion.
It also notes that the influence of the in situ formed carbides on biocompatibility remains unexplored and would merit further investigation.

paper_did: Synthesized an equiatomic CrMoNbTiZr high‐entropy alloy (HEA) from elemental Cr, Mo, Nb, Ti, and Zr powders using powder metallurgy in an argon‐filled glove box followed by spark plasma sintering at 1200 °C under 40 MPa in vacuum.

Characterized the resultant alloy’s microstructure by X‐ray diffraction and SEM/EDX, identifying a dual‐phase microstructure (a BCC matrix with a discrete Laves phase) along with in situ formed carbides.

Evaluated mechanical properties including global and phase‐specific Vickers microhardness, room‐temperature compressive behavior (yield strength, ultimate compressive strength, and elastic modulus), and analyzed fracture features.
Assessed tribological performance via sliding wear tests using an alumina ball to determine coefficient of friction, wear scar morphology/depth, and wear rate.

Investigated electrochemical behavior through potentiodynamic polarization in simulated physiological media (PBS and Hanks’ solution), determining corrosion current densities, passivation characteristics, and related localized corrosion phenomena.
paper_reported: The SPS‐processed CrMoNbTiZr HEA achieved approximately 97% of theoretical density and exhibited a dual‐phase microstructure consisting of a BCC matrix and Laves phase (as predicted by CALPHAD), with additional carbide formation due to reactions with the graphite die.

Mechanical testing revealed a global Vickers microhardness of about 531 HV (with the Laves phase at ~642 HV and the BCC phase at ~365 HV), a high compressive yield strength (~1111 MPa) and ultimate strength (~1236 MPa), and an elastic modulus (~35 GPa) comparable to that of cortical bone.

Tribological analysis showed a coefficient of friction of ~0.43, a wear scar depth of approximately 47 µm, and a low wear rate (3.4×10⁻⁴ mm³/Nm), with wear mechanisms identified as abrasive and adhesive in nature.

Electrochemical measurements in PBS and Hanks’ solution demonstrated good corrosion resistance, featuring low corrosion current densities and distinct passivation behavior, with localized corrosion primarily observed in Mo‐rich regions.
paper_proposed: Future work suggestions include employing additional processing steps (e.g., hot isostatic pressing) to further densify the alloy and reduce surface porosity that can serve as crevice sites.
Applying homogeneous heat treatment to improve elemental diffusion and reduce micro‐segregation.
Investigating the possible positive role of in situ formed carbides on biocompatibility, even though their influence on HEA biocompatibility was not explored in the current study.

paper_did: Prepared two high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) based on the CoCrFeNiMo system: one Zr‐free (Sample 1) and one doped with 0.71 wt.% Zr (Sample 2) via vacuum arc remelting with repeated remelting for homogenization.
Characterized the microstructure using SEM, EDS, and XRD to reveal a dendritic structure with grain refinement (notably in Sample 2) and the presence of secondary phases such as a Cr–Mo rich σ phase.
Measured mechanical properties by performing three‐point bending tests to determine the Young’s modulus and conducted microhardness testing.

Conducted corrosion evaluations in a 3.5% NaCl solution via linear polarization, potentiodynamic polarization (yielding Tafel slopes and corrosion rates), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess passive film resistance and overall corrosion behavior.

pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The findings of the paper that demonstrate work-hardening effects under CE (PMC11378927::web::014) and the role of selective phase corrosion in degradation.
pool.what_is_new: Introducing a pre-treatment mechanical work-hardening step to deliberately induce an adaptive protective layer that mitigates the synergistic interplay between wear and corrosion, a strategy not explored in the referenced study.

fields.hypothesis: The resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in HEAs is governed by an adaptive work‐hardening mechanism where the preferential removal of the softer FCC phase under mechanical impact induces a dense, strain‐hardened surface layer that improves passive film formation and reduces localized corrosion.
fields.material_initial_state: As-cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase microstructure, featuring a softer FCC matrix interspersed with harder intermetallic σ and μ phases.
fields.intervention: Apply a pre-conditioning mechanical treatment (e.g., controlled shot peening) to pre-induce nanocrystallization and work hardening in the FCC matrix at the surface prior to exposure to combined wear and corrosive environments.
fields.conditions: Testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under cyclic cavitation erosion (CE) conditions comparable to those described in the paper.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined, strain-hardened surface microstructure with improved passive film repair dynamics.
fields.mechanism: The intervention accelerates the formation of a dense work-hardened layer by intensifying dislocation density in the FCC phase. This layer better withstands mechanical removal, supports a robust passive oxide film, and minimizes the formation of microcracks at phase boundaries that normally serve as corrosion initiation sites. Consequently, a synergy between wear-induced work hardening and corrosion resistance emerges.
fields.predicted_outcome: The pre-treated sample will exhibit a reduced cumulative mass loss (both from mechanical wear and corrosion-induced degradation) when compared to the untreated baseline by approximately a moderate margin (direction supported qualitatively by increased hardness data and passive film stability, although precise values are uncertain).
fields.baseline: As-cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA without pre-treatment exhibiting conventional CE-induced selective phase corrosion as described in PMC11378927::web::012::morphologies_and_roughness_of_cocrfenimo.
fields.boundary: This mechanism should hold when the wear intensity is sufficient to activate work hardening in the FCC phase but not so high as to remove the entire surface layer; it might fail under extreme CE conditions that prevent any passive film recovery.
fields.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in mass loss and distribution of strain-hardened phases is not precisely known.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of as-cast HEA samples—one group will receive shot-peening to induce surface work hardening while the other remains untreated. Subject both groups to identical CE tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution with periodic electrochemical noise and mass loss evaluations.
measurements: Surface microhardness (Vickers)
Passive film integrity (via OCP shifts and EN analysis)
Cumulative mass loss and surface roughness over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in cumulative mass loss and improved passive film stability compared to the untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: The paper’s findings on the impact of selective phase corrosion at microstructural boundaries (PMC11378927::web::023::ce_mechanism_of_cocrfenimocu0_1_hea) combined with literature on the benefits of microstructural homogeneity for corrosion resistance.
pool.what_is_new: Advocates for a post-casting homogenization heat treatment to target the microstructural origins of aggressive localized corrosion under wear conditions—an approach that directly tackles the interplay between microstructural heterogeneity and passive film stability not addressed in the original study.

fields.hypothesis: The resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the stability and uniformity of the passive film, which critically depends on microstructural homogeneity; homogenizing the microstructure via post-casting solution treatment can eliminate compositional gradients and intermetallic precipitates that serve as weak links for passive film breakdown.
fields.material_initial_state: As-cast HEA with heterogeneous microstructure featuring compositional segregation and pronounced intermetallic phases (σ and μ) interspersed within the FCC matrix.
fields.intervention: Apply a post-casting solution treatment (homogenization annealing) process to dissolve or reduce the intermetallic phases and achieve a more uniform single-phase FCC microstructure.
fields.conditions: Carry out cavitation erosion-corrosion tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution under conditions similar to those in the original study.
fields.structural_mediator: A homogenized microstructure with minimized chemical inhomogeneities that supports a more continuous and defect-free passive film.
fields.mechanism: The solution treatment minimizes local compositional differences and removes or reduces the size and quantity of intermetallic precipitates. This uniform microstructure reduces the formation of micro-galvanic cells and sites of preferential passive film breakdown under mechanical stress, thereby enhancing the overall resistance to concurrent wear and corrosion.
fields.predicted_outcome: The homogenized HEA should display improved resistance against both mechanical erosion and corrosion, reflected by lower cumulative mass loss, more stable OCP behavior, and less severe surface pitting compared to the as-cast condition. The extent of improvement is directionally supported by literature but quantitatively uncertain.
fields.baseline: As-cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA with its inherent microstructural inhomogeneities and intermetallic phase segregation, as characterized in PMC11378927::web::009::microstructure_characterization_of_cocrf.
fields.boundary: The effectiveness of the solution treatment is contingent upon sufficient homogenization without over-softening the material; under conditions where complete dissolution of intermetallics is not achieved, the benefits may be reduced.
fields.uncertainty: Exact improvement metrics (e.g., mass loss reduction percentage) are uncertain and need experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one in the as-cast state and the other subjected to a controlled homogenizing solution treatment. Expose both sets to identical CE-corrosion testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution while characterizing passive film integrity, microstructural homogeneity, and mass loss over time.
measurements: Phase distribution via EBSD/SEM-EDS
Electrochemical measurements (potentiodynamic polarization, EN)
Cumulative mass loss and surface morphology analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the solution-treated samples do not demonstrate significantly lower mass loss and improved passive film stability compared to the as-cast samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: observations in the paper that the as-deposited coating exhibits surface porosity that eventually becomes partially filled by a passivating film, implying a potential regulatory role for porosity in corrosion behavior (PMC8305802::web::013).
pool.what_is_new: It proposes to control and optimize surface porosity via a sealing treatment, thereby directly linking engineered surface morphology to dual-mode degradation resistance—a concept not explored in the original work.

fields.hypothesis: The extent and distribution of surface porosity, inherent to the electro spark deposition process, govern the combined wear–corrosion resistance by serving as initiation sites for localized passivation film formation, which under controlled sealing conditions reduces both degradation modes.
fields.material_initial_state: A CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating produced via electro spark deposition on 316L stainless steel, characterized by a slightly porous upper layer with exposed splats.
fields.intervention: Apply a post-deposition surface sealing treatment (such as plasma-assisted or chemical sealing) to fill and smooth out the outer porosity, thereby optimizing the morphology for secure passivation layer development.
fields.conditions: Subject the sealed and unsealed coatings to an accelerated wear–corrosion test in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution with controlled abrasive action (e.g., particle impact or sliding wear apparatus).
fields.structural_mediator: A sealed, low-porosity surface that minimizes stress concentration sites and micro-crevices where corrosive agents can accumulate, leading to more uniform formation of protective passivating films (likely rich in Cr oxides).
fields.mechanism: Surface porosity in the as-deposited coating can act as stress concentrators and corrosion cell sites; however, when these pores are sealed, the resultant smooth surface allows the passivation film to form uniformly and more effectively acts as a barrier against both mechanical abrasion and electrolyte penetration. This reduces localized corrosion and mechanical wear channel initiation.
fields.predicted_outcome: The sealed coating is predicted to show lower rates of material loss under combined wear–corrosion conditions (evidenced by reduced wear track roughness and lower corrosion current density) compared to the unsealed baseline. The improvement should be evident in both decreased pit formation and diminished abrasive damage.
fields.baseline: The unsealed CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating with inherent porosity from the ESD process.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be beneficial in environments where the sealing remains intact; under extreme mechanical loading that fractures the sealed layer, the advantage would be lost. It may also be less effective if the sealing treatment induces detrimental residual stresses.
fields.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement is uncertain and likely depends on the effectiveness and durability of the sealing treatment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings: one subjected to a post-deposition sealing treatment to close surface porosity and a control group left unsealed. Expose both groups to simultaneous wear–corrosion tests using a saline abrasive setup.
measurements: Surface morphology analysis (SEM) to confirm porosity sealing
Wear track analysis (profilometry)
Electrochemical measurements to assess corrosion rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sealed coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in both wear damage and corrosion indicators compared to the unsealed coating, or if sealing adversely affects performance, then the mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: Leverages the paper's demonstration of grain refinement and dynamic amorphization under sliding while introducing controlled cyclic loading to optimize the trade-off between wear-induced nanocrystallization and time-dependent recrystallization/passivation in corrosive settings.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a programmable sliding regimen to dynamically maintain an optimal ultra-nanocrystalline state that enhances both mechanical and chemical resilience, directly linking shear rate programming with concurrent improvements in corrosion resistance.

fields.hypothesis: The resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by a dynamic balance between grain refinement and limited recrystallization in the surface layer, such that continuous cyclic shear maintains an optimal ultra-nanocrystalline state that promotes rapid surface passivation.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA produced through additive manufacturing with initially large grains (~42 µm) that undergo severe shear-induced grain refinement during sliding.
fields.intervention: Implement a programmed sliding regimen with carefully timed cycle durations and pause intervals in a corrosive (chloride-rich) environment to regulate the balance between dynamic nanocrystallization and recrystallization of the surface layer.
fields.conditions: Tribocorrosion experiments at ambient temperature in a chloride electrolyte where sliding cycles (and intermittent stops) are varied to modulate the extent of grain refinement versus time-dependent grain growth (recrystallization) and passivation film repair.
fields.structural_mediator: A continuously renewed ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer (grain sizes in the 2–10 nm range) that maintains high concentrations of active grain boundaries, which enable both low friction (via inverse Hall-Petch mechanisms) and rapid formation of protective oxide patches.
fields.mechanism: During cyclic sliding, the surface evolves through rapid grain refinement due to high shear, which lowers friction through inverse Hall-Petch softening. However, pauses allow limited recrystallization and grain growth, which can temporarily increase the surface hardness. In a corrosive environment, freshly exposed high-energy grain boundaries rapidly form oxide passivation patches. By programming the cycle duration, the dynamic equilibrium can be tuned to favor a persistently refined, passivated surface that resists both mechanical wear and corrosive attack.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline sample having a continuous, unmodulated sliding regimen (e.g., constant cycling without pauses or with excessively long pause times), the optimized cycling condition will display lower steady-state friction, reduced wear rates, and decreased corrosion current densities. The improvements should be evident at moderate loads where the dynamic balance can be maintained.
fields.baseline: A control HEA sample tested under continuous sliding without controlled pause intervals, leading either to excessive grain growth (diminishing rapid passivation) or poorly managed wear rates.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under conditions where the time scales for shear-induced grain refinement and thermally driven recrystallization are suitably separated. If pauses are too long (allowing extensive grain growth) or if the sliding cycle is too aggressive (preventing oxide repair), the protective effect may fail.
fields.uncertainty: The precise interplay between cycling time, grain refinement kinetics, and passivation dynamics in a corrosive environment is complex, and the optimal timing parameters require careful calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple groups of HEA samples subjected to tribocorrosion tests under different programmed sliding regimens—for example, continuous sliding versus controlled cycling with varied pause durations. Characterize the surface microstructure (grain size distribution via TEM), passivation quality (using XPS), and record friction, wear, and corrosion data.
measurements: Surface grain size distributions (TEM)
Thickness and quality of oxide passivation (XPS)
Steady-state friction coefficients
Wear volume (profilometry)
Corrosion current densities (electrochemical tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples under optimized cyclic sliding do not show a statistically significant improvement in maintaining an ultra-nanocrystalline, passivated surface along with reduced wear and corrosion compared to the continuous sliding baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.builds_on: the finding that trace boron enhances the formation of beneficial, fine TiB2 particles (as in the paper) and its relation to improved hardness and wear resistance, extending that concept to explain simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance through passive film stabilization.
pool.what_is_new: It explicitly links the nanoscale dispersion of in situ ceramic precipitates with dual performance against wear and corrosion, proposing that a uniform ultrafine particle distribution under controlled boron addition enhances the adhesion and stability of the passive film, a mechanism not specifically isolated in the paper.

fields.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy coating produced by laser cladding with no or excessive boron addition, leading to either coarse or inhomogeneously distributed TiB2.
fields.intervention: Introduce a precisely controlled, trace amount of boron (near x = 0.5) during laser cladding to yield a uniform dispersion of ultrafine TiB2 precipitates.
fields.conditions: Coatings are produced under identical laser cladding parameters, with only the boron content adjusted to target ultrafine particle formation in a harsh corrosive mechanical environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl with imposed sliding wear).

The refined grains further contribute by creating more grain boundaries that can slow corrosion pathways and impede crack propagation under cyclic mechanical loading.

fields.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in wear rate and corrosion current is uncertain, though the trend is expected to follow the comparative improvements seen in the optimized S2–S3 compositions reported in the paper.

Coefficient of friction (COF)
Corrosion current density (icorr)
Microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS and XRD to assess particle size/distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized coating does not show a statistically significant improvement in both wear rate and corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or worse icorr and wear rate than the baseline), or if microstructural analysis shows no difference in TiB2 dispersion, the hypothesis would be falsified.

fields.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy coating with in situ formed TiB2 particles produced by laser cladding, which in its as-cladded state may exhibit suboptimal particle–matrix bonding and localized defects.

fields.predicted_outcome: Annealed coatings will display reduced adhesive wear (with fewer spalling events) and lower corrosion rates (evidenced by lower icorr and improved passivation film stability) when compared to the as-cladded baseline.
fields.baseline: The as-cladded HEA coating with in situ formed TiB2 particles, which may suffer from weak particle–matrix bonding and associated degradation under combined mechanical and corrosive stresses.

In environments where heat-induced phase transformations occur or where the annealing atmosphere is not controlled, the benefit may be negated.
fields.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvement in interfacial bonding is expected to lower wear and corrosion degradation, the precise extent of reduction in degradation rates is uncertain due to process sensitivity.

Subject one batch to an optimized post-cladding annealing treatment and keep the other as-cladded. fields.predicted_outcome: The annealed/HIP-treated HEA samples will exhibit a lower combined degradation rate (both wear and corrosion) compared to as-deposited samples, with a measurable improvement (uncertain magnitude) in passive film continuity and coating thickness retention.
fields.baseline: As-deposited LMD HEA coatings that show manufacturing cracks and discontinuous passive films (e.g., Mo-HEA on carbon steel, as reported in PMC8200011::web::003 and PMC8200011::web::015).
fields.boundary: The protective effect should be significant under moderate erosive conditions and in fluids where passive film formation is operative; however, at extreme mechanical impacts or highly aggressive chemical conditions, the benefit may diminish.

fields.hypothesis: The resistance of HEAs to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the quality of the interface between the HEA coating and its substrate, where a graded interlayer reduces galvanic potential differences and improves stress transfer, thereby minimizing localized degradation.
fields.material_initial_state: HEA coatings deposited via LMD on substrates with significant differences in thermal expansion and composition (e.g., carbon steel vs. stainless steel), which can lead to interfacial microcracks and galvanic effects.
fields.intervention: Introduce a compositionally graded interlayer between the substrate and the HEA coating (or adjust deposition parameters to achieve a graded interface) to better match the thermal expansion coefficients and reduce electrochemical potential differences.
fields.conditions: Conduct comparative tests on samples with and without graded interfaces under simulated geothermal environments that impose both corrosive chemical attack and mechanical erosive loads.
fields.structural_mediator: The integrity and electrochemical compatibility at the HEA/substrate interface, as evidenced by reduced microcracking and minimized galvanic coupling.
fields.mechanism: A graded interlayer minimizes sharp compositional and thermal expansion mismatches that lead to microcracking and localized galvanic corrosion (as observed in the carbon steel–HEA interface in PMC8200011::web::017). Improved interface integrity will reduce the initiation sites for combined damage from wear and corrosion. By reducing interfacial defects, the passive film continuity over the entire coating-substrate system is maintained under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
fields.predicted_outcome: HEA coatings with a graded interface will show lower interfacial crack densities, reduced galvanic corrosion indicators (e.g., less iron-based corrosion product formation), and lower overall combined degradation compared to coatings deposited directly on a dissimilar substrate.
fields.baseline: Traditional LMD-deposited HEA coatings on substrates with abrupt compositional and thermal mismatches (e.g., Mo-HEA on carbon steel, which exhibited galvanic effects in PMC8200011::web::017).
fields.boundary: The effectiveness of the graded interface is expected to be most pronounced when the substrate mismatch is substantial. In cases where the substrate is already compatible (e.g., stainless steel), the graded layer may offer marginal benefits.
fields.uncertainty: While the role of substrate compatibility is well understood, the quantitative impact of a graded interlayer on simultaneous wear and corrosion under dynamic geothermal conditions remains to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA-coated samples: one with a compositionally graded interlayer at the interface and one without. Expose both in a controlled apparatus reproducing geothermal conditions with simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., high-velocity fluid jets).
measurements: Interface microstructure assessment (using cross-sectional SEM)
Detection of galvanic corrosion indicators (via EDS mapping of corrosion products)
Quantitative assessment of overall wear-corrosion damage (thickness loss, pit formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graded-interface samples do not demonstrate reduced interfacial degradation (microcracking, galvanic corrosion markers) and improved overall wear-corrosion resistance compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
